rationale: A wins because it stays closer to what Ramp can actually prove while giving the founder five usable lanes, especially “Ramp puts an AI agent to work on vendor contracts, but a human still hits send.” B has real craft, but “The first AI agents in finance departments aren't doing the math — they're writing the awkward emails” is a faceplant: the update says the agent scans spend and flags unused seats, so yes, it is doing the analytical work. A has a couple of small stretches; B has one angle built on a contradiction. That is how decent work loses to disciplined work.
gaps_in_A: “They came from cancelling” overstates the update; the facts say savings were mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not that cancellation drove realized savings.
“plans to charge enterprises later” is an inference from “enterprise tier,” not a stated fact. Usable, but it needs to be marked as a question until pricing is confirmed.
The vendor-side angle uses “across a large spend base” with Ramp's $80B purchase volume but does not ask how much of that is software spend. A reporter will.

The refused angle “Ramp's enterprise tier signals a new phase for AI in finance” is killed a bit too hard; it is weak as standalone news, but it could support the governance angle if the workflow details are real.
gaps_in_B: “The first AI agents in finance departments aren't doing the math” is invented and partly false. The update explicitly says the agent scans spend and flags duplicate and unused seats.
“Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions” overclaims the action. The agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails; finance approves them.
“SaaS pricing has depended on customers not auditing their own seat counts closely” is a broad market claim with no proof in the update. Good instinct, unsupported sentence.
Primary next step “newsjack-detector” is less useful than resolving proof and fit-checking the data angle. This is a launch with a strong internal number, not a reactive newsjack yet.
